title: By the river Chebar (Ezekiel 1)
hook: among exiles in Babylon, a vision of a chariot of fire and wheels

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king burned Jeremiah's scroll, and the prophet and Baruch wrote it all again, with more. Today, a new prophet, far from home.
screen: `THERE WERE ADDED BESIDES UNTO THEM MANY LIKE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Where does God live? For many in Judah, the answer had an address: Jerusalem, the Temple, the holy of holies. Now some of them have been carried off to Babylon. They sit by the river Chebar, a long way from that address. Among them is Ezekiel, whom the text calls a priest, far from the Temple where priests serve. And his book opens there, in the King James words: "as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God." Not in Jerusalem. In exile.
screen: `GOD HAD AN ADDRESS.` → `CAPTIVES BY THE RIVER CHEBAR.` → `THE HEAVENS WERE OPENED.`

segments.voice: What Ezekiel sees is hard to describe, and he knows it. A whirlwind comes out of the north, a great cloud, fire folding in on itself, a glow like bright metal at the center. Out of it come four living creatures, each with four faces: a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. They have wings, and they move straight ahead without turning. Beside them are wheels, as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel, their rims full of eyes. Wherever the spirit goes, the wheels go too. Above is a firmament like crystal, then a throne, and on it a figure like a man, surrounded by brightness like a rainbow in the clouds. Listen to how careful the language is. Ezekiel almost never says this is what it was. He says the appearance of, the likeness of, as it were. At the top, he piles them up: "This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD." Three layers of distance before the name of God. Jewish tradition calls this vision the merkavah, the chariot. The Mishnah treats it with great caution: it is not to be taught even to one student, unless he is wise and already understands on his own. Mystics later built a whole path of contemplation around it. But the plain meaning is enough for today. The throne has wheels. The glory that seemed tied to one building shows up beside a river in a foreign land, right there with the exiles.
screen: `A STORM, FOUR LIVING CREATURES.` · `A WHEEL IN THE MIDDLE OF A WHEEL.` · then, large: `THE APPEARANCE OF THE LIKENESS OF THE GLORY.` · then: `THE THRONE HAS WHEELS.`

segments.voice: If you can, go to a window or step outside, and find something in motion: a cloud, a bird, branches, even a ceiling fan. Just watch it move, without naming or explaining it; Ezekiel was standing in an ordinary place, by a river in a foreign land, when the sky opened. If you pray, you can pray from right where you are, the way the exiles had to.
Merkavah. The chariot: the name Jewish tradition gives to Ezekiel's vision of the throne with wheels, seen among exiles by the river Chebar. Today's word.
Your line: God in exile too. The throne has wheels, and it came to the river. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 1 as the opening of the book of Ezekiel, and in many communities it is chanted as the prophetic reading on the first day of Shavuot.

fork.setup: you're Ezekiel, a priest far from the Temple. the sky opens over a river in Babylon. how do you describe what you see?

describe it as the appearance of a likeness.

chat.says: Why does it matter that Ezekiel saw his vision in Babylon, not Jerusalem?
options: It shows God's glory wasn't tied to one building; it came to the exiles by the river.
It shows the exiles had forgotten Jerusalem and no longer cared about the Temple.
It means Babylon's gods had sent the vision, since Ezekiel was in their land.
chat.meaning: By the river Chebar the heavens opened over the captives. The throne has wheels: the glory shows up beside the exiles, far from the Temple.

merkavah.meaning: the chariot: tradition's name for Ezekiel's throne vision

notes: The word 'merkavah' does not appear in Ezekiel 1; the script presents it as the name tradition gives the vision. Keeper may want to confirm framing.
Mishnah Chagigah 2:1 is paraphrased: the chariot is not expounded even to one, unless he is wise and understands on his own. Please check the 'single student' wording.
Ezekiel 1 as the haftarah for the first day of Shavuot appears only in howItsDone; Keeper please confirm.
'Mystics later built a whole path of contemplation around it' refers to merkavah/hekhalot mysticism; kept general by design.
The opening of Ezekiel 1:1 includes a date ('the thirtieth year'); the script leaves it out.

Editor: the text says 'river of Chebar', so 'canal' became 'river' throughout; the Mishnah Chagigah 2:1 paraphrase now says 'not even to one, unless he is wise' instead of 'only to a single student'; cut 'a Tuesday'.
